name: 7 - Inviting, Summarizing and Responding to Public Comments Transcript
content:
WEBVTT
 
 Beth S. Noveck: 7th in…
 
 Beth S. Noveck: on using AI to improve and enhance and accelerate how we do citizen engagement. As part of that, we have heard quite a bit from different projects. People like the City of Hamburg, who have spent 3 years building a back-end analytics toolkit
 
 Beth S. Noveck: to analyze citizen comment. We're gonna hear very soon about how, Google Jigsaw and the City of Bowling Green have worked together to do something similar.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Today is a little bit more, shall we say, quick and dirty. We want to talk about what it is that you can do without spending 3 years designing or building a system.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: what it is that you can do, what you can't do, what's safe to try, and what you might do for yourself, and where you might start experimenting. So, we want to answer the question, what can I do right now?
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So we're going to try to focus on both explaining and understanding the use of AI for both summarizing comments, for synthesizing comments.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: We want to talk and leave some time specifically to talk about rulemaking comments.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And so I think we'll segregate those two, because rulemaking has some very specific rules, and if time allows, we'll try to cover some other areas of the waterfront about uses of AI to promote engagement, and other things that our speakers want to bring in. Okay, so without further ado…
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Let me start to the conversation here. And we really want to hear from you and maybe Bill, as the public servant here and the longtime government worker, what are some of the challenges that you have faced
 
 Beth S. Noveck: When it has come to processing public comments. And how did you use AI to help you overcome those challenges? So we'll start with a very concrete example, and then we'll go from there.
 
 William Zipse: Sure, I mean, I'll be,
 
 William Zipse: honest with you, I don't do as much rulemaking, but working in forestry in a state like New Jersey, where, if you're not familiar, New Jersey has about 9 million people, but the state's about 5 million acres, 2 million of which are forested.
 
 William Zipse: So, we always try… we try to engage the public and tell them, you know, as much about what we're doing and try to get input as much as we can.
 
 William Zipse: And a lot of the challenges, we try to involve a lot of, different groups in the state that represent different aspects of the public, because we manage a lot of public land. And one of the processes was, we're kind of short-staffed.
 
 William Zipse: Like a lot of government agencies, and it's a big job trying to vet the diverse opinions in New Jersey. New Jersey, in terms of just its landscape, from the north end of the state to the south end, is very different in terms of even its forests, and why people use them, and how they use them.
 
 William Zipse: So, you know, we would get lots and lots of comments in, and we really… we would like to be able to use those to inform the decision-making, and have the public involved, and have a real say in terms of… of, you know.
 
 William Zipse: what the… in terms of what those comments mean for the management of their land. So, that's always been a challenge. You're up against real-time constraints, permitting, all kinds of other things. You have staff working on analysis, getting things done in the field. So, being able to actually use those public comments and… and…
 
 William Zipse: be able to get through them, sometimes that takes the entire amount of time that you have for input. So we were trying to use, artificial intelligence in a way that would kind of streamline that and give us the ability to be, more responsive to public comment and be able to incorporate it into our management better.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Maybe I'll just ask you, Bill, to real quick tell us briefly the story of how you… because this… really, this session is organized around you. You are the hero of this session, in the sense that I know, don't worry, I'm gonna put you on the spot here, but you were the one who, went out and just
 
 Beth S. Noveck: went and did something. And that's what we want to hear about for a moment, because this is… this is what people are here to learn about. What could I just go out and do? And then Michael and Alex will tell us why we should not try this at home.
 
 William Zipse: Well, I mean, I will be… yeah, so my first experiences with this actually didn't have to do with forestry directly. They had to do with parks, but we do a lot of biometric and analytical work.
 
 William Zipse: on the forest, and so I had a team that was interested in doing this type of work.
 
 William Zipse: And there happened to be a very, very tight comment window. The first time we did this was with Liberty State Park.
 
 William Zipse: There's a number of projects going on there, and fortunately for us, sort of the way it was arranged was pretty interesting. They had different categories of projects, and had had different surveys around those different categories of projects, and then another overall survey
 
 William Zipse: And then, interestingly enough, there had been in-person sessions where comment cards were collected, and people reviewed those cards for, like, their content and their, and their sentiment. And then there were online comments, a lot more online comments, where they didn't have people review
 
 William Zipse: What those comments contain in terms of sentiment.
 
 William Zipse: Or, or, you know, their content. So, the idea was there was this public meeting coming up, and our administration really wanted a synopsis of what those comments said, and if there was anything in there that they might have missed that might be interesting to mention in the public meeting, and it was going to be a packed public meeting.
 
 William Zipse: So we were kind of lucky in that case. We had a training data set.
 
 William Zipse: We had sets where people had actually gone through these comments and taken a subset of them and vetted them. Now, there were a couple complications with that.
 
 William Zipse: Happy to speak to that if people are interested in it, because, you know… but that was sort of our first experience with it, and the plan was that, originally, to go through those comments, the administration was going to hire
 
 William Zipse: some part-timers and have them go through the comments, and the estimate was, like, 3 months to go through them. But there was this series of public meetings leading up to where that 3 months… where they're gonna announce some of these results in that… after that 3 months.
 
 William Zipse: that it, you know, our administration said it'd be nice to be informed, so what could you do? So I had… I happened to have a team working on some biometrics at the time for another project, and we kind of diverted and… and did the analysis.
 
 William Zipse: And in about a day and a half, we had a pretty good idea of what those comments contained. And then we did run some rudimentary… rudimentary, traditional analysis, so we cross-validated the results.
 
 William Zipse: Using the training data from the comment cards. So that's sort of how we used it, and some of the things I would say were an advantage in Liberty, where it shined was a lot of the,
 
 William Zipse: A lot of the surveys were very much unstructured, asking people their opinions about specific projects, so sorting that would take a very long time.
 
 William Zipse: So, being able to go through that.
 
 William Zipse: you know, with AI helping to summarize and having that subset of data was really helpful. It was kind of interesting, though, because with one of the things that the,
 
 William Zipse: the, the subset of data that we had, the training data, sentiment, like, AI is… the AI at the time, this is GPT 3.5 era, so before reasoning models and all that kind of stuff, at least in our hands, it was not very good at picking up on sentiment.
 
 William Zipse: And those of you from New Jersey know Jersey sarcasm, right? So, somebody may, oh yeah, I can't believe they're putting this in the train station, that's a great idea! Well, that's… that's not a positive comment, but, you know, AI might pick that up. I said it was great! So, also, one thing that was kind of humorous during that whole
 
 William Zipse: that whole, evaluation was there was a developer who had a lot to do with the project, and his last name was Fireman.
 
 William Zipse: So whether people liked this person or not, you know, the large language model picked up on that people had very strong opinions about the fire department in the neighborhood, because they didn't know to make the distinction that that was somebody's name.
 
 William Zipse: So it's kind of interesting to see those sort of successes and failures, and kind of be aware, because at best, with sentiment, it was about… we did cross-validate, it was about 60… a little over 60% accurate at doing that, so again, something to be leery of.
 
 William Zipse: And then, for… we also had another project with, Wharton State Forest.
 
 William Zipse: And this was much more narrow in scope for the AI side of things, but those of you who have
 
 William Zipse: been in southern New Jersey know there are a lot of sand roads, it's very flat and sandy, and they've been around for a long time, and
 
 William Zipse: there's, there was… there are a lot of different names for the same roads, and they're colloquial. So there's this database of all these…
 
 William Zipse: road names for the same places that can be joined in this geo… geo-geographic information system. And the idea was to go through all that open-ended
 
 William Zipse: unstructured language and pick out those road names and join them, and then look for spatial patterns. So that… that was kind of a more traditional approach. It wasn't trying to extract meaning from any of those comments. The other thing I'll just point out is, like.
 
 William Zipse: you know, some of… some of the structure of the, surveys and how the comments are taken is very, very important. And I see a lot of questions coming in from people about, you know, fairness, and so whatever direction you'd like to take it from here, Beth, or…
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Great. I'm gonna… I wanna bring in our other discussants here, but I want to encourage people, we can kind of do this in three dimensions, you know, we can answer some things on the chat as we go, and we'll talk as we go. Michael, let me go over to you, and Michael has a really extraordinary background. The environmental connection is obviously very serendipitous here, but Michael's also, I want to shout out, has been really one of the,
 
 Beth S. Noveck: pioneers in the field of computational law, and the use of AI and other technologies, also for legal analysis, and really thinking about how we can analyze texts with AI.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So, let me go over to you and kind of ask you first how you see, the role of AI changing how governments process and understand comments, and we'll stay away from rule… again, let's stay away from rulemaking for the moment, because that has special rules. And really, this question, and I'm going over to you, Alex, like.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: we've heard words like sentiment, we've talked about opinions, we've talked about… there's different content in comments, sort of what's working, what's not working, what do you see as being the most promising? So for public servants here, what's the most promising thing they could go out and try, and what should they not try?
 
 Michael A. Livermore: All right, great. Well, thanks for the invitation to be here. It's always really interesting to hear how some of these, tools are playing out on the ground. So, this kind of goes… builds on what you were saying, Beth. You know, there's…
 
 Michael A. Livermore: comments in any kind of proceeding, rulemaking or in any other public proceeding, are just very complex things, right? And they contain lots of different kinds of information.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: So, and at the end of the day, that's what you're trying to do with any kind of text analysis tool, is extract useful information, and then summarize it, present it in some way, because the problem with comments, the problem, is that there's just so much, so many of them, there's so much information, so what you're trying to do is you're trying to take this, like, firehose of information, and then, you know, narrow it down, remove the extra.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: and then, you know, lift out what's most interesting. So this… it's kind of a refinement process in some sense, right? And so this can operate at different levels. You know, Beth and I worked on a project several years ago with, having to do with public comments.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: And, you know, one of the major issues is that you get a lot of duplicate comments, right? There's just the same thing over and over and over again. Now, you might want to keep track of how many of those there are, right? That's useful, like, you know, a thousand people wrote in and said that, you know, with, like, a postcard that also the same thing, and they said they don't like this idea, or they love this idea, or whatever it is. You might want to keep track of it, but
 
 Michael A. Livermore: You know, you don't need to read.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: over and over and over again, the same thing a thousand times, right? And so, just that de-duping, which I don't know if we would call that artificial intelligence, but it's a computational, you know, NLP natural language processing tool, can be extremely… that just as a first cut, can be extremely useful. Now, we talk about AI, large language, of course, that's an ambiguous term, so a lot of term, large language models, maybe we're talking about.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: But with… with something like a large model, large language model, you might be able to, and we could talk about specifically how you do all this stuff, it's like, you know, that's technically kind of complicated, but you might be able to do, like, a kind of a more coarse-grain
 
 Michael A. Livermore: version of deduping, right? So the first version is just, if it's identical, down to the last period, and then you can kind of coarse grain out from there to say, look, if it's largely, it's 90% the same, or whatever else, you can have different gradations of deduping.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: So that's… so that's one thing that you can do. I'll just very, very quickly offer another, tool that has been used in different public commenting process.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: Is, topic modeling.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: It's a very different operation with topic modeling. So deduping, you're just trying to get out the, kind of, the chaff at some level. What you would then use a topic model to do, if you had a very large number of topics, is to essentially summarize
 
 Michael A. Livermore: the main themes that are present in the topic. It provides you, kind of, with a 30,000-foot view of the landscape.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: And then some ways of maybe picking out representative comments to say, okay, this is a cluster of themes, and here are some comments that are, you know, right in the middle of that cluster. So I'm going to look at those. Say you can't read every single comment, right? Or you're not going to be able in a timely fashion. Or there's going to be some that you might read in a more in-depth way, because it represents a cluster of ideas that's very prevalent in the text.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: Those are both kind of pre-GPT approaches. I'll leave it there. We can talk about GPT, too, and there's a gajillion things to talk about. But I think the main theme is this idea that
 
 Michael A. Livermore: There's a lot of information in public comments, and what you're often trying to do with these tools is refine out the useful information, and so that's where you're going to reach for that tool to work in your context.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Let me go over to Alex and ask you the related question, and maybe another gloss on that, which is, what's the question we should be asking?
 
 Beth S. Noveck: to which we're going to get responses that lend themselves to summarization with AI.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And in the meantime, what I'm also gonna do is, there's a very practical question, Bill, of just, like, what product did you use? So I'm just gonna put that question in the chat and ask you to respond in writing, while Alex talks, as maybe you could just do the, like, what tools did you use thing. But sort of same question back to you. What is AI really good for? How do we deal with these different issues?
 
 Beth S. Noveck: deduplication, bucketing, summarization, etc. What do you see as being the most promising applications right now?
 
 Alexander Spangher: So, so I was gonna mention exactly what Michael mentioned as well, which is that there are also classical approaches, like topic modeling, but let me, let me start by saying,
 
 Alexander Spangher: well, hello to everyone, thank you for having me on. I, before doing my postdoc and then PhD, I was a journalist at the New York Times, and I, worked a lot with a lot of these tools every day. This was 10 years ago now.
 
 Alexander Spangher: And as many of you know, journalism is suffering, so I left to get my PhD so that I could ostensibly save local news.
 
 Alexander Spangher: And so that's what my PhD focused on. I wanted to kind of forward a whole list of,
 
 Alexander Spangher: let me see if I can send this, just, like, resources and papers. So, a couple of things that I want to start with is just,
 
 Alexander Spangher: if you're gonna use LLMs with summarization or anything, I would really pay attention to benchmarks that exist.
 
 Alexander Spangher: That's the first thing I sent. This is one benchmark, the GEM benchmark. A great friend of mine who's now at Bloomberg, is totally responsible for this benchmark, but it's… there are benchmarks for pretty much many, many, many things that you want to measure. And I would not
 
 Alexander Spangher: Jump into, kind of.
 
 Alexander Spangher: a use case for LLMs without checking, like, what the benchmarks are saying, doing, or modeling. Second thing I want to say, classical approaches to summarization, topic modeling is very near and dear to my heart. We use this a lot at the New York Times, and there are now modern extensions of topic modeling that allow you to
 
 Alexander Spangher: Forum topics for many different things you might want to study or ask.
 
 Alexander Spangher: I remember the public editor came to us at the Times and said, listen, I want to summarize all of the reader comments that are coming in, and I want to get a view of what the readers are complaining about, on a week-to-week basis. And we use topic modeling for that.
 
 Alexander Spangher: So…
 
 Alexander Spangher: the reason why I would, again, plus one on that is that it's cheap, it runs on your computer, you don't share data with the cloud, and there's a lot of theory that backs up it, that is doing, kind of, this maximal information aggregation.
 
 Alexander Spangher: Third thing I want to say with the links that I forwarded is that,
 
 Alexander Spangher: We think a lot about, also, prioritization. So, information… can we pull out the comment that is maybe the most important comment, quote-unquote? Or can we take a batch of comments and route them
 
 Alexander Spangher: to the right people. And so the first link I forwarded, the EPA comment prioritization link, is a link that, Dan Ho did in my lab.
 
 Alexander Spangher: where they worked very closely with both the EPA and the US, as well as the similar organization in Chile, to develop routing pipelines to send comments to the right people and escalate complaints to the right people.
 
 Alexander Spangher: I have similar work in trying to detect the most newsworthy lead, or the most newsworthy policy that's being discussed in a city council meeting.
 
 Alexander Spangher: I would just kind of close on that by saying that, prioritization is often… we say summarization a lot, but, like, prioritization is also, like, a very important
 
 Alexander Spangher: way of getting a sense of what the public is saying, because so many comments are… are not necessarily, kind of.
 
 Alexander Spangher: part of, like, the pool we might want to summarize. I mean, often we want representative comments, and… and…
 
 Alexander Spangher: ways of thinking about this, classifiers to prioritize comments is something that I feel like should be a very important part of the conversation.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: By the way, if at any point anyone wants to disagree with, one another or add anything immediately, please do, please do let me know here.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So, I think what I see from the questions that are coming in already is just a push towards really concretely understanding, kind of, what… what… coming back to this, what can we do? So you've told us we have to check the benchmarks, Alex, we have to understand what, what's kind of reasonable to expect. Can you put this in sort of very concrete terms, or maybe…
 
 Beth S. Noveck: anyone else, whether it's Michael or Bill, sort of… I'm gonna come back to this question of what's the question?
 
 Beth S. Noveck: That I can ask, sort of, what am I… what should I… so we have policymakers here in different roles, people doing service delivery, whether it's, I'm asking for comments on how to improve this service I'm delivering, or I'm doing a planning exercise of the kind that build it. Do you see certain areas of, let me call it governance or policymaking, that are going to lend themselves better?
 
 Beth S. Noveck: To what people can do without a large-scale, kind of.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: 3-year Hamburg style, or Ben is here from Bowling Green, we maybe will hear from him a little bit about how long it took to roll out his project, you know, what they can do for themselves.
 
 William Zipse: Yeah, I mean, I think…
 
 William Zipse: I think there is some potential. I think you do have to be cautious with how you use these. You know, looking at some of the surveys, for example, you know, not… we didn't design the surveys, but I do sample design for forests, and looking at those and saying, hey,
 
 William Zipse: you know.
 
 William Zipse: If I had designed that sample a different way, it would have been much easier to extract different types of information. Certainly some of the quantitative aspects of it. But I would say one thing that, to me, was pretty impressive, you know, managing forests, I'm, you know.
 
 William Zipse: how we… how we usually work internally with other disciplinary, you know, interdisciplinary management, or working with people from other domains, a lot of time what we'll do is we'll design these silvicultural prescriptions, forestry prescriptions, but, like, a biologist may not necessarily speak the language of forestry, so we conduct simulation work.
 
 William Zipse: And the thing that I found was really, really interesting was some of the comments that would normally kind of, I think, get glossed over. Like, some people put in these heartfelt letters, but when you went through them, you're like, wow, there's a couple good ideas in there. Or if somebody made comments about, like, what the art should look like at Liberty State Park, like.
 
 William Zipse: Again, it's not AI making the decision, it doesn't have taste in terms of, like, art, but, like, bringing something to your attention, and you can get that in front of somebody who knows about that subject.
 
 William Zipse: And I did find that really, really interesting. I mean, not even knowing about all the different aspects of some of the topics that were brought up, you know, it was much, much faster and easier to get things where somebody brought up a really original idea.
 
 William Zipse: Or something that they put a lot of effort into writing about, like, that normally, if you were going through comments, you get this letter along with the comments.
 
 William Zipse: it takes a long time to process that normally, and really read through it, but you could right away know, okay, this letter is dealing with, you know, how somebody feels about how the art space is being handled at Liberty. Let's get this in front of the person that handles the art space.
 
 William Zipse: And see what their thoughts are on this. You know, so, like, I think that's where it shows… for me, it showed a lot of potential, and in the forestry world, how I would use that is, you know, there's a lot of…
 
 William Zipse: There's a lot of sense… there's a lot of, sometimes people come up with really good ideas that you wouldn't necessarily think of, in terms of how they want their forest managed.
 
 William Zipse: Or they might come back to you with something they feel really strongly about, with which, through my forester's perspective, I might not have seen the value in that, but it draws my attention to it. Not that the AI knows about that value, but it draws my attention to it. So I think, what Michael was saying before, kind of using it as sieves, like, you can use it as different…
 
 William Zipse: styles of sieves and kind of cut your data different ways. You just have to be careful in taking really, really complex things, like
 
 William Zipse: You know, classifying people, for example, and boiling that down to a class, right? Like, that's the danger with classifying anything. But, you know, AI makes that so easy. You know, LLMs make that so easy based on very complex and nuanced language.
 
 William Zipse: So just, you know, being careful with that. But in terms of off-the-shelf things people could use, I think there are a lot of LLMs out there, that are very easy and cheap… they're very easy and cheap to access.
 
 William Zipse: And, you know, now machine learning toolkits are very, very accessible, you know, much more so than they were in the past decade. So there's a lot of ways that you can experiment with this. My advice
 
 William Zipse: Going into that, though, is I'd pick something where you already have publicly available data, because, you know.
 
 William Zipse: take as little risk as possible in the beginning, and give yourself room to fail. Because, like, you know, it's gonna… each model is different. I think we were talking about this in the waiting room, that
 
 William Zipse: you know, every time a new model comes out, how that model handles and classifies these things is different. I see there's a lot more… a few more questions coming in here about the technical side, which I can… which I can,
 
 William Zipse: answer in the chat if you'd prefer, but… Yeah, I mean, in terms of the work stack, I feel like…
 
 William Zipse: You know, if people want to summarize, like, large documents quickly, I mean, even playing around with, like, Google Notebook LM, right? That can do some amazing things. It has this mind map tool that makes these graphical maps that can refer to these documents, and you can look through them. Just, I would say.
 
 William Zipse: the only caution… well, a big note of caution to that is just, it makes it so easy, just be aware of, like, what might be missing from that. So, you know, as you're going through these documents, I did find,
 
 William Zipse: You know, there was some discussion on, you know, sort of…
 
 William Zipse: how does it represent comments that were repeated over and over and over again? And sometimes it almost feels like some of the minority comments, because the combination of words and tokens was unusual, those got a lot of weight. Like, they rose to the surface pretty quickly. So you kind of have to balance out, like.
 
 William Zipse: you know, all these comments that came in that said the same thing versus unique material, but I think it is very, very good for getting to… you know, you can use a lot of off-the-shelf tools to get to, you know, really unique or heartfelt comments much easier than was possible before.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So let's go over to Michael and then to Alex, and I think there's a lot of questions coming in, sort of asking for more specifics on, sort of, if I wanted to go out and do deduping first, exactly what does that mean, and how would I do that? If I wanted to go out and do topic modeling,
 
 Beth S. Noveck: sort of more… more guidance on how to do this, where you need a bespoke tool, or where you can, again, sort of DIY it for yourself.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And are there other strategies that you would recommend? I'm going to kind of keep pushing on this question, to… in the hope that we can help people come away from this understanding one thing they can try for themselves.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: Okay, good, yeah, so I mean…
 
 Michael A. Livermore: Alex might have some more specific ideas about, like, which tools to use and stuff. I mean, what I do is I find a graduate student to work with.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: Come on.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: That's how I usually… because this stuff changes, and then if that doesn't work, honestly, what I do is I go to ChatGPT, and I say, hey, you know, I'm kind of thinking about doing this.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: And so… and it really depends a lot on your level of technical expertise, like, are you comfortable programming in Python, or is that just, like, something that is never gonna happen, right? And so… or R. So it just… it just… it's very, very context-specific. Now, if you're talking about a deduping tool.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: you know, you can Google.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: deduping, right? And, like, you're… and you're gonna get lots of hits from that. And what you're doing with deduping, just to clarify, is, you know, if there are, you know, say you got 10,000 comments in, but, you know, maybe 2,000 or several thousands of those are exact copies of each other, deduping is just…
 
 Michael A. Livermore: you know, finding duplicates and identifying those duplicates. And there are different tools to do that. It's actually not quite as obvious and easy as it sounds, because
 
 Michael A. Livermore: often they're not exact copies of each other, and so what you're going to be looking for are things that are pretty close copies of each other. And then what you would ideally do is retain out,
 
 Michael A. Livermore: you know, whatever is unique in the comments. So that's what de-duping is, and if you have a mass comment campaign, if there's an organization that goes out and collects lots of comments, but they're all exactly the same, again, you want to keep track of that, but you don't have to want to read through them all in order to figure that out. The point that Bill made about
 
 Michael A. Livermore: You really gotta watch out for that, by the way, because if, like, 10,000 people write in, and they all say the same thing, and then two people write in and say something weird, you don't want to focus on those two people. Like, you might want to, maybe they have an interesting idea, but the fact of the matter is that the… a lot of the opinion was on the other side, right? And so if, like, 10,000 people love the idea, and 2,000 people vehemently hate it, you know, you don't want to just give equal weight to those. You might, I don't know, I guess it's your decision, but
 
 Michael A. Livermore: there's reasons not to give equal weight to that, right? And so you have to be very careful about understanding exactly the information that you want. Like, again, this gets to your kind of point, Beth, is like…
 
 Michael A. Livermore: What you can't do, which would be awesome, is go to ChatGPT, give it all of your comments, and say, hey, tell me what is useful in these comments, right? That you can't do. The technology isn't even remotely there to do that. So what you have to do instead is you have to really think about, okay.
 
 Michael A. Livermore: What am I gonna do?
 
 Michael A. Livermore: here, and I don't want to read every single comment, right? So what I want to do is then use some of these tools to take some of the load, so if the starting plac
 
 [... truncated ...]
